meta.title: Who really said "Coming together is a beginning, staying together is progress, working together is success"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Popularly pinned on Henry Ford, but there's no evidence he said it. The earliest documented use (1927) credits Edward Everett Hale — though even that lacks a primary source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Coming together is a beginning, staying together is progress, working together is success'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Henry Ford. The earliest documented source credits Edward Everett Hale via a 1927 U.S. presidential budget address — the Ford tag appears only in 1949.

answer.label: Not Henry Ford — credited to Edward Everett Hale
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Henry Ford ever said or wrote this. The earliest documented appearances — including President Coolidge quoting it in a 1927 U.S. budget address ↗ — credit Edward Everett Hale, though even Hale’s original source has never been located. The Ford tag surfaces only in 1949.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: Together — one of the most inspiring words in the English language. Coming together is a beginning; keeping together is progress; working together is success.
trail: Quote researcher Barry Popik ↗ traces the earliest documented use to a 1927 U.S. budget address in which President Coolidge credits Edward Everett Hale, and finds the Henry Ford version only from 1949.
Wikiquote records the line under Hale, sourced to a 1920s presidential address, and notes it has been misattributed to Ford — see the Talk:Edward Everett Hale ↗ discussion.
The fuller “Together — one of the most inspiring words…” wording is catalogued under Hale at LibQuotes ↗, citing the presidential budget address.
Popular quote sites still print it as Ford’s — e.g. QuotePark ↗ — which is how the misattribution keeps spreading.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version drops the opening line — and Hale’s name
source.excerptNote: As quoted by President Calvin Coolidge, who introduced the sentence with “Edward Everett Hale said…” The now-common form swaps “keeping together” for “staying together.”

source.rightsNote: The wording predates 1929 and appears in a U.S. Government publication (a presidential address), so the text itself is in the public domain. Authorship, however, is unsettled: it is credited to Edward Everett Hale but no source in his own writing has been found.

author.name: Edward Everett Hale
author.kicker: The name in the earliest record
author.heading: Edward Everett Hale
author.bio: Edward Everett Hale (1822–1909) was a Boston-born author and Unitarian minister, best remembered for the 1863 story The Man Without a Country. A grandnephew of the patriot Nathan Hale and nephew of the orator Edward Everett, he was a prolific essayist and reformer who served as Chaplain of the U.S. Senate from 1903 until his death. He is the earliest figure on record credited with the “coming together” lines — although no source in his own writing has ever been pinned down.

cite.sourceCitation: Calvin Coolidge, “Address of the President of the United States and the Director of the Bureau of the Budget at the Second Semiannual Meeting of the Business Organization of the Government,” June 10, 1927, quoting Edward Everett Hale. Earliest documented appearance of the saying; no original source in Hale’s own works has been located.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly pinned on
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s most durable teamwork “Henry Ford” quotes — printed on posters, slide decks and LinkedIn posts. The paper trail does not support it.

items.why: No source in Ford’s writings, interviews or speeches has ever been produced. According to Barry Popik’s research ↗, the Ford attribution does not appear until 1949 — two years after Ford’s death — long after the line was already in print crediting Edward Everett Hale, and “there is no evidence to suggest that he either originated or popularized it.”

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented attribution is to Edward Everett Hale, quoted in a 1920s U.S. presidential budget address ↗ — not Henry Ford. Even Hale’s own authorship, however, rests on that second-hand crediting rather than a located original text.

context.heading: Why the line traveled
lead: The sentence entered the public record not as folksy business wisdom but as a plea for coordinated government. President Coolidge deployed it in a 1927 address to the “Business Organization of the Government” — the era’s budget-efficiency meetings — introducing it as something “Edward Everett Hale said.”

Detached from that setting, the three tidy clauses were perfect for reuse, and over the following decades they drifted onto motivational lists. By mid-century the prestige of the Ford name had attached itself to the words, and the original speaker was forgotten.
